doc.title: Eddie Miller and Pete Fountain Interview, 1970-01-09

title: Old New Orleans sheet music and record company control
summary: A caller suggests reviving old New Orleans jazz publications; Pete says record executives want current hits.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Record labels, producers and the business of making albums

blocks.x: That's good. Thank you. Thank you. Go ahead, please. You're on close-up.

I'd just like to say I come from a family in New Orleans that has nothing to do with jazz. In fact, they were mostly concert people and so forth. But in my young days, I used to see that there was so much jazz music published in New Orleans. And, of course, I might be giving this away to somebody else. But if Pete would get somebody to go back in and try to dig this stuff out and, you know, modernize it a little bit, I think he'd have some jump numbers and so forth that would really shock this whole nation.
I have a couple books on that. Some of the old-time rag things. But it's just so hard to get to. And it's so hard to get your A&R man, which is out of California. On.

and your recording studio to sell them on this idea. Oh, really? Yeah, sometimes, you know, they say, no, this is what's selling now, and this is what's, you know, and most of the times I do, really, I have to do the songs that they think's going to sell. Oh. You know, years ago I could do, but all of a sudden, you know, they put their clamps on it, you know, they just, like we're doing more of the modern tunes. Yes, I know. But one of these days I want to get my own recording studio, so then I can do what I want to do.
Yeah, then you can push it.
Right, then I can play some of the old songs or just modernize them, which I think you're right there, it could be done.
Modernize them, and because some of these people have some good ideas, I think.

Thank you. You know, that's something that Jerry Mulligan talked about when he was down here. He'd like to take some of those old ragtime tunes and rearrange them for the ten-piece bands that he sometimes records with. I think there'd be a market for that kind of thing. I think he'd get into the bank. Yeah. Hello, go ahead, please.
